text: Getting the right alert to the right team at the right urgency, which the last lesson covered, isn't the end of the story. The page itself still has to hand the responder something useful. This lesson covers what a real runbook contains, and the real convention for attaching one directly to an alert.

A page that just says an alert is firing tells you something is wrong and almost nothing about what to do next. If this exact alert has fired before, someone on the team probably already knows the cause and the fix — but that knowledge usually lives in one person's memory, or a Slack thread nobody can find at two in the morning. A runbook attaches that knowledge directly to the alert, so the responder doesn't need the history to act.

A good runbook is a focused document meant to be read in the first two minutes of an incident, not a general wiki page. It covers what the alert actually means in plain language, the specific diagnosis steps to check first and in order, known fixes that have genuinely resolved it before — a rollback, a restart, a failover — and an escalation path naming exactly who to contact if the first responder can't resolve it in time.

The real convention for attaching that runbook is a runbook_url annotation set directly on the alert rule. In a Prometheus alert for a high error rate on checkout-api, that annotation sits alongside a plain-language summary, and Alertmanager carries both straight through into whatever channel fires — Slack, PagerDuty, email — so the link sits right next to the page itself, not in a separate system the responder has to remember exists.

It's worth being precise about one distinction: a runbook is not a postmortem. A runbook is written before an incident, as a prepared response to a known failure mode, and stays mostly static until a new fix is discovered. A postmortem, covered in Chapter 7, is written after one specific incident to analyze what happened and drive follow-up work. A team that only writes postmortems re-learns the same lesson every time that alert fires again; a team with only runbooks never improves the underlying system, just the response to it.

That closes out dashboards and alerts: build panels around real signals, visualize them across both clouds in Grafana, route and deduplicate the resulting alerts so the right team gets paged without burning out, and hand every page a runbook instead of a bare alert name. Next, the chapter shifts from reliability to what all of this actually costs.
